intro: Till rides through a market, impersonates a priest and makes fools of learned professors before the law catches up with him. The United States Navy Band plays Strauss’s tale in Herb Weber’s transcription, with a winding tune and a sharp little laugh identifying the rogue through every disguise.

cues.title: Once upon a time
cues.text: The tale begins gently in F major. A winding tune soon introduces Till, and a shorter, sharper figure gives him his laugh. These two shapes keep returning as the music sends him through one scrape after another.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey describes the prologue and two Till motifs. James Hepokoski, Framing Till Eulenspiegel, 19th-Century Music 30.1 (2006), discusses the opening F-major complex, bars 1–111. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A horn and a laugh
cues.text: Strauss gives Till two very different introductions: a winding horn tune and a clipped clarinet figure. The horn seems to be telling a story; the clarinet can puncture it in a few notes. Their rhythms survive the disguises that follow.
cues.evidence: Dotsey identifies the two themes and their original horn and clarinet scoring; Hepokoski discusses bars 6–20 and 46–49. This note describes Strauss’s themes, not a new instrumental entrance at this time.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: A good laugh
cues.text: Asked many years later whether Till has any “metaphysical” intentions, Strauss replies: “Oh, no—I only wanted to give the people in the concert hall a good laugh for once.”
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, quotes Strauss’s later answer to a question about metaphysical intentions in the piece. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/

cues.title: The trickster in print
cues.text: The old Eulenspiegel stories send their rogue from town to town, upsetting princes, clergy, craftsmen and scholars. Their earliest surviving written accounts come nearly two centuries after the fourteenth-century life assigned to him. Strauss gives this well-travelled troublemaker a new ending: the gallows.
cues.evidence: Dotsey distinguishes the legendary fourteenth-century biography, later written accounts and Strauss’s execution scene. Hepokoski, pp. 8–9, discusses the Volksbuch tradition and Till’s death in bed in the earlier tales.

cues.title: A horse in the market
cues.text: Till rides straight through the market women. Strauss punctuates the ride with a cymbal crash and flutter-tongued trumpets, turning the scene into a shrieking commotion. The escape ends in a sudden gap: Till’s seven-league boots carry him away.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the cymbal crash, flutter-tongued trumpets and escape pause. The composer’s programme labels for bars 135 and 151 are reproduced in Hepokoski, Table 1, p. 13.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The rogue dresses as a priest
cues.text: Till’s priestly disguise comes with a comfortable B♭-major tune, its phrases neatly paired. The little laughing figure keeps peeping through. Soon the music darkens: even Till can imagine where his mock sermon might lead.
cues.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 24–25, analyses the B♭-major pastor episode, bars 179–207, including its paired phrases. Dotsey describes the clarinet interruption and the ensuing fear motif in muted brass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dainty courtesies with pretty girls
cues.text: Strauss’s own label for this scene is Till “exchanging dainty courtesies with pretty girls”. Delicate violin and woodwind solos carry the flirtation. Till falls for one of the girls, and the music grows more ardent as he woos her.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the violin and woodwind solos, Till’s infatuation and his wooing. Strauss’s labels 12–14 (bars 209–232) are listed in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Mary Whittall’s translations in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A refusal, then a vow
cues.text: The girl rejects him politely, and Strauss’s label puns on the German idiom for a rebuff: “However fine, a basket still signifies refusal.” Till is furious. The orchestra cuts off, and four horns play his theme in unison as he vows revenge on all mankind.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the rebuff, Till’s fury and the four horns in unison. Strauss’s labels 15 and 17 (bars 244 and 263) are in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Whittall’s translations in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The professors lose the argument
cues.text: The professors arrive in A minor. Till poses his outrageous questions, and their answers multiply in a fugato: one part starts a phrase, another imitates it, and more voices pile in. Strauss makes scholarship sound wonderfully flustered.
cues.evidence: Strauss’s letter to Franz Wüllner, 20 October 1895, identifies the A-minor episode and fugato; quoted and discussed in Hepokoski, pp. 10–11 and 27. Dotsey describes the bassoon and bass-clarinet portrayal of the professors.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A grimace from afar
cues.text: Having set the professors a few outrageous problems, Till leaves them baffled. From a distance he turns back for what Strauss labels a “big grimace”: one long, dissonant chord for the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the departure and the long dissonant chord. Strauss’s labels 19 and 20 (bars 315 and 345) are in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Whittall’s translations in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Whistling a street tune
cues.text: Strauss calls the tune “Till’s street ditty”: a jaunty melody that could have come from an operetta by one of the other Strausses. The whistling soon falls silent, and a still, ominous passage follows.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the whistled tune and the ominous silence after it. Strauss’s label 21 (bars 375–382) is in Hepokoski, Table 1, with Whittall’s translation in note 23. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nuts for the Cologne audience
cues.text: On 20 October 1895 Strauss writes to the conductor Franz Wüllner: “This time let’s let these folks themselves crack the nuts that the rogue delivers to them.” Wüllner conducts the première in Cologne on 5 November.
cues.evidence: Strauss to Wüllner, 20 October 1895; James Hepokoski’s translation in Framing Till Eulenspiegel, pp. 10–11 and note 18. Première date on p. 4. https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf

cues.title: The winding tune returns
cues.text: After the uneasy quiet, Till’s winding tune comes back. Earlier themes crowd together as the pace grows wilder. Even the priest’s decorous melody will be swept into the rush, blazing out in D major just before the arrest.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes the return of Till’s horn theme and the accelerated priest music. Hepokoski, pp. 33–37, traces the reprise from bar 429 and the priest theme’s D-major return at bars 567–572.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The drum calls court
cues.text: A drum roll stops the merriment. Heavy brass confront Till in F minor, and his short replies still try to make a joke of the proceedings. The jokes give way to fear. Strauss takes the scene all the way to the hanging.
cues.evidence: Hepokoski, p. 37, identifies the drum roll and ff F-minor trial from bar 577. Dotsey describes the brass, Till’s replies, the returning fear motif and the execution.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A strangled clarinet
cues.text: The sentence is carried out. Strauss’s label in the score reads: “Up the ladder! There he swings, the air is squeezed out of him, a last jerk.” A strangled clarinet depicts the hanging.
cues.evidence: Dotsey identifies the strangled clarinet. Strauss’s label 26 (bars 615–619) is in Hepokoski, Table 1, in Whittall’s translation (note 23). https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/ ; https://jameshepokoski.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/2006-Framing-Till-Eulenspiegel.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The story outlives the rogue
cues.text: The gentle opening returns in F major, as though the storyteller has closed the book. Strauss lets the phrase continue where it once broke off. Then Till’s mischievous figures jump in for one last, unruly ending.
cues.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 37–38, relates the epilogue at bars 632–657 to the opening and identifies the F-major cadence at bar 636. Dotsey describes the final interruption by Till’s motifs.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A cymbal crash breaks the tiptoeing
transitions.from: A · A tale begins in F major
transitions.to: B · On horseback through the market
transitions.how: Till’s tune breaks into short, quiet fragments. A cymbal crash releases the market scene, with flutter-tongued trumpets among the rushing notes. The little pieces of his theme now propel a stampede through the market.
transitions.evidence: Dotsey’s score account describes the quiet fragments, cymbal crash and trumpet effects. Hepokoski, Table 1, locates the ride at bar 135. https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-till-eulenspiegel/

transitions.title: The priest settles into B♭ major
transitions.from: B · On horseback through the market
transitions.to: C · A priest’s tune in B♭ major
transitions.how: The escape leaves a gap before the priest’s tune begins. Its measured, paired phrases settle into B♭ major, marked gemächlich — at ease. The wind chords give it a sober bearing, though Till’s laughing figure soon interrupts the sermon.
transitions.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 24–25, gives the B♭-major pastor episode, gemächlich and paired phrases in bars 179–194. Dotsey identifies clarinet and bassoons among the original score’s instruments and describes the motif’s interruption.

transitions.title: Till’s horn tune breaks the stillness
transitions.how: The quiet, held passage gives way to the winding horn theme. Strauss restores the opening’s F-major world and its quick, off-balance phrases. The theme starts moving between parts again, gathering the players into another crescendo.
transitions.evidence: Dotsey identifies the still interlude and return of the signature horn theme. Hepokoski, pp. 33–35, maps the return at bar 429 to the opening, followed by the renewed crescendo from bar 449.

transitions.title: The drum roll interrupts D major
transitions.to: E · The trial in F minor
transitions.how: The priest’s tune blazes out in D major. A diminished-seventh chord and a fortissimo drum roll cut across it, bringing the trial’s heavy F-minor brass. Till answers these imposing statements with short, exposed scraps of his own music.
transitions.evidence: Hepokoski, p. 37, describes D major in bars 567–572, the diminished-seventh chord, drum roll and F-minor trial at bar 577. Dotsey describes the brass statements and Till’s replies.

transitions.title: F major after the gallows
transitions.from: E · The trial in F minor
transitions.how: After the execution, six separated F-major chords dwindle from piano to pianissimo. The opening phrase then returns at half speed, marked Doppelt so langsam. It reaches a gentle F-major cadence and continues into the longer epilogue.
transitions.evidence: Hepokoski, pp. 37–38 and 40, identifies the six F-major impulses in bars 624–631, the epilogue at bar 632, its marking and the cadence at bar 636. The original string pizzicato is described here as separated chords for this band performance.

composer.epithet: The son of a horn player, he gave the orchestra a taste for scandal and the soprano some of her longest, loveliest farewells.
facts: Munich, with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer; conducting with Hans von Bülow at Meiningen
Munich · Weimar · Berlin Court Opera, 1898–1918 · Vienna State Opera, 1919–24
Tone poems, fifteen operas, two horn concertos and more than two hundred songs
composer.background:
Richard Strauss grew up with the horn in his ears. His father Franz played in the Munich Court Orchestra, including the first performances of Wagner’s Tristan and Die Meistersinger, and detested the music. At home, Mozart stood above everybody; Haydn and Beethoven were safe too. Richard, born in 1864, had piano lessons from the age of four and was composing at six. His mother Josepha came from the Pschorr brewing family. He studied privately with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer and learnt the sound of an orchestra from the men his father worked beside.

Hans von Bülow took him to Meiningen in 1885. At twenty-one he had an orchestra of his own to rehearse, as well as a choir and a princess to teach. The violinist Alexander Ritter, married to Wagner’s niece, completed his conversion to the music his father disliked. Ritter also urged Liszt’s symphonic poems upon him. Strauss would spend the next decade finding out how much a concert orchestra could tell us about a man without letting the man sing.
